articles.title: US Navy quietly removes top commanders, draws congressional backlash
articles.summary: The US Navy has quietly removed or fired several senior officers and officials in recent months without its customary public announcements, drawing
articles.body: The US Navy has quietly removed or fired several senior officers and officials in recent months without its customary public announcements, drawing criticism from lawmakers over a lack of transparency and failure to inform Congress about key personnel changes.Two Democratic lawmakers on Thursday accused the Navy of withholding information about the removal of the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine following an underwater collision last month. Separately, the Navy also dismissed the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East in September, while its attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court departed amid an internal investigation.The developments mark a departure from the Navy's longstanding practice of publicly announcing the removal of senior commanders and other high-profile officials. They also come amid growing restrictions on the release of information about US military operations, particularly in the Middle East.In a letter to acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and the service's top uniformed officer, Adm. Daryl Caudle, Democratic Reps. Joe Courtney of Connecticut and Adam Smith of Washington expressed concern over the Navy's failure to notify the House Armed Services Committee about the dismissal of the commander, second-in-command and top enlisted sailor of the USS South Dakota submarine.The lawmakers said the three officers were removed after the submarine struck an unidentified object on the seabed. However, the Navy declined to publicly comment on the incident or the subsequent personnel action.“As a result of the Navy’s failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy’s commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress,” the lawmakers wrote.The letter also expressed “deep frustration” over the Navy's failure to inform the committee about the submarine leadership changes.Destroyer commander removed amid Iran operationsIn a separate development, the Navy on September 27 relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham of her command of the USS Michael Murphy destroyer, which has been deployed to support operations against Iran, according to a defence official who spoke on condition of anonymity.Cunningham was removed due to a loss of confidence and had held the position for less than a year, the official said.The Navy did not publicly announce her removal, even when questioned about the personnel change. Such dismissals are typically disclosed within days, marking another departure from the service's usual communication practices.Navy physician departs amid investigationThe departure of Rear Adm. Dr Brian Monahan, who served as the attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, has also drawn attention.Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California confirmed his departure on Thursday but provided few details about the circumstances.The Navy has opened an investigation into the matter, according to a person familiar with the situation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss it.Monahan served for nearly 18 years as the head of the Office of the Attending Physician, which provides emergency medical assistance to members of Congress and the Supreme Court, as well as congressional staff and visitors.He had previously attracted public attention for discussing the health of Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell and administering a Covid-19 vaccine to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.Growing restrictions on military informationThe developments come amid broader restrictions on the disclosure of information about US military activities, particularly in the Middle East.US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the region, has released limited details about recent strikes on Iran. It has also declined to comment on the extent of damage to military bases and equipment, frequently citing operational security concerns.Access to satellite imagery has also faced restrictions. Major satellite imagery providers holding US government contracts have blocked or delayed the public release of images from the region at the request of American officials.These restrictions have made it difficult to assess the impact of Iranian attacks on US military installations. An Associated Press analysis found that it took months to establish that Iranian drone and missile strikes had damaged or destroyed structures at 26 military bases and other sites housing US equipment across the region.The Navy's handling of the recent personnel changes could also become an issue during next week's confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, who is seeking permanent appointment as the service's top civilian official.You use AI every day. articles.title: Australian billionaire Nicola Forrest donated around $500 million to her new foundation; the money will support Indigenous children and women entrepreneurs
articles.summary: Australian billionaire Nicola Forrest has donated more than $500 million to her Coaxial Foundation in 2026, with the funding supporting initiatives for
articles.body: Australian billionaire Nicola Forrest has donated more than $500 million to her Coaxial Foundation in 2026, with the funding supporting initiatives for Indigenous children and female entrepreneurs. The donation, comprising $125 million in cash and 25 million Fortescue shares, has enabled the foundation to announce its first three major long-term partnerships. These include up to $30 million for venture firm Antler to support up to 250 Australian female founders, $30 million over six years for Cape York Partnership to fund early learning initiatives for Aboriginal children, and $7.1 million over three years for SNAICC to improve early childhood learning outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.Nicola Forrest’s foundation announces its first three major partnershipsCoaxial Foundation announced its first three major long-term partnerships as part of its commitment to expanding opportunities for women and children. The foundation said the partnerships were selected to support organisations with the expertise and experience needed to create lasting change.The announcement includes an up to $30 million partnership with Antler, a $30 million commitment to Cape York Partnership over six years, and a three-year partnership worth $7.1 million with SNAICC. These initiatives will provide funding, investment opportunities and programme support across entrepreneurship, early childhood learning and family development.Antler partnership will provide funding and business support to women foundersOne of the foundation's major commitments is an up to $30 million partnership with Antler, a global early-stage venture firm. The partnership will support up to 250 Australian female founders by providing access to funding, business networks and support during the early stages of building their companies.According to Coaxial Foundation, the partnership includes up to $10 million in non-dilutive funding, co-investments and programme support over four years. It also includes a $20 million investment into Antler Australia Fund III. The initiative aims to help female founders access the capital and resources required to develop their businesses.The partnership will also establish Momentum, powered by Coaxial, a dedicated four-year programme designed to identify, fund and support female founders. It will combine Antler's global venture platform with funding and investment support from Coaxial Foundation.Forrest’s foundation backs early childhood development in Cape YorkCoaxial Foundation has committed $30 million over six years to Cape York Partnership, an organisation working with Aboriginal communities. The funding will support learning and development initiatives for young Aboriginal children in the Cape.The partnership forms part of the foundation's broader commitment to improving opportunities for Indigenous children and families. Through the initiative, Cape York Partnership will receive long-term financial support for its work in early childhood learning and development.SNAICC partnership aims to strengthen early learning for Indigenous childrenThe foundation has also announced a three-year partnership worth $7.1 million with SNAICC – National Voice for our Children, the national peak body for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and families.The funding will be provided through grants and philanthropic support to strengthen SNAICC's ability to support early childhood learning outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children across Australia. The partnership will focus on helping the organisation extend its existing work with Indigenous families and communities.Coaxial CEO Philippa Watson said the foundation's partnerships with Cape York Partnership and SNAICC were long-term commitments to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and families. She said the initiatives would provide children with access to early learning opportunities that could be scaled to strengthen family systems and improve outcomes.Forrest outlines her vision for long-term philanthropic investmentNicola Forrest said the partnerships reflected her belief that philanthropy could act as an initial catalyst for change, while sustainable improvements required long-term investment and support.In the official media release, Ms Forrest said: "Australia does not have a shortage of talent, ambition or people committed to making things better. Too often, what is missing is access to opportunity, capital and the sustained support required to turn potential into outcomes."She also highlighted the importance of working with experienced organisations and maintaining long-term commitments. Reflecting on her experience in business and philanthropy, she said: "Thirty years in business and philanthropy have taught me that good intentions are not enough. Lasting change requires strong partners, evidence, disciplined execution and the willingness to stay the course."Coaxial Foundation said the three partnerships were among its first commitments following Forrest's initial donation of more than $500 million. The foundation described the announcement as the beginning of a broader programme of long-term investment in initiatives intended to create meaningful impact.You use AI every day.
